summary: Implementation phase (Rob via Miles, 2026-10-30). Done: EVM source BB-42 to BB-45, EVM supply reporting BB-58, frontend BB-59 and BB-60, XRPL BB-55 to BB-57 (local branch, PocketIC passing), Solana BB-48. In Review: BB-47 (Solana components). In progress on Sonnet: BB-49 (Solana lanes; fixes being tested) and BB-51 (Sui Move gate; CLI download awaits approval). BB-46 held; BB-27 waits on Rob. Nothing merged, deployed, signed or enabled.

glossary.definition: Code or documents exist and were inspected. This alone does not show the bridge running.
Automated checks passed on a developer’s computer. This does not show a live transfer.
Connected components were exercised in a local test environment, with simulated parts identified. This is not public-network proof.
First round of independent review. The reviewer found problems, which were fixed in a later code version.
Second round of independent review. It found a mint transaction gas allowance that was too small.
Third round of independent review. This reviewer passed the candidate and noted a minor scheduling issue that was then fixed.
First round of independent review, not release version one. This reviewer found problems that were subsequently fixed.
Second review round. It found a possible double payment and a background timer that could fail to restart.
Third review round. It found incorrect runbook read commands and missing limits on incoming request sizes; both were fixed.
The work item that inspected the existing token contracts. Here R1 is part of a reconnaissance task ID, not a review verdict.
An initial investigation of existing code before choosing what to reuse or change.
The toolkit used to build and test the Base token contract.
Foundry’s command-line program; forge test runs the contract’s automated tests.
Automated checks run by the code-hosting service. The listed local tests are separate evidence.
The smart-contract execution system used by Base and Ethereum.
Create tokens. This bridge creates Base tokens only after canonical Rumi tokens are reserved as backing.
Permanently remove tokens. A Base bridge burn creates a claim to release the matching backing on ICP.
The older token’s loan-repayment operation. It is not the new bridge’s return-transfer operation.
Requests to blockchain data services for chain information or transaction submission.
Replace-by-fee: replace a pending transaction with a higher-fee transaction using the same transaction number.
An account’s transaction sequence number. Reusing the correct number helps prevent duplicate execution during replacements.
An accounting rule that must remain true, such as token claims having enough backing.
Tokens accounted for against borrowing debt. The new escrow-backed bridge keeps separate books.
Canonical icUSD held aside to cover bridge tokens and pending claims.
The ICP ledger standard used to retrieve transaction records and verify what a transfer actually did.
The description of a canister’s callable methods and data formats, used to generate matching app bindings.
Generated app files that describe how to call the canister’s published interface.
The wallet-provider interface used by the web app to request Ethereum-compatible wallet actions.
Content Security Policy: browser rules controlling which outside connections the app is allowed to make.
An ICP wallet whose approval flow must be respected when the app requests signed calls.
Canisters that a wallet session has been authorized to call. Adding the bridge may require reconnecting an existing session.
The Ethereum-compatible transaction format used here, including its gas and fee fields.
The byte-encoding format used to assemble Ethereum-compatible signed transactions.
A fixed reference example with a known expected result, used to detect encoding changes.
A Foundry command-line tool used to independently check transaction encoding and calculated values.
The local Ethereum-compatible test blockchain used to execute bridge transactions without public-network funds.
A standardized form of an ECDSA signature, used here so signed transactions have the expected encoding.
The required agreement between blockchain data providers before the bridge accepts a result.
The latest block accepted as finalized by the configured provider checks, rather than a newly announced sequencer block.
Reading blockchain events in bounded batches so a large response does not stall the bridge.
A blockchain record showing whether a transaction executed and which events it produced.
A change to the chain’s previously observed block history; unsettled work must be checked again.
Related state changes are recorded together, so only part of the update cannot be left applied.
The ledger’s time window for recognizing a repeated transfer request as the same request.
A ledger storage canister containing older transaction records.
The compiled executable installed in an ICP canister.
The compiled executable after size-reduction processing; this is different from proving it was installed.
A local ICP test environment used to run canisters and exercise their interactions.
Threshold ECDSA: ICP network nodes collectively sign the bridge’s Base transactions.
A test supplies a controlled answer instead of obtaining it from a real outside service.
End-to-end tests that exercise a complete local bridge flow across connected components.
The check that observed Base token supply exactly matches the bridge’s accounting when no transfers are in flight.
The exact-supply reporting check for a quiet bridge; the fixes avoid false mismatch reports.
A tested attack scenario: extra tokens are created outside the bridge’s records, then burned to try to withdraw backing.
A previously skipped test now runs normally and must pass.
The automated test runner used for the bridge web app.
The app’s Svelte and TypeScript checker. At baseline means the bridge added no new reported issues.
Base’s public test network. No bridge deployment or transfer there has been authorized or proved.
An action is waiting for separate authorization; a completed code task does not authorize deployment or funds movement.
An independent reviewer actively looks for ways the implementation could fail or violate its requirements.
The reviewer found no blocking issue within the stated scope and exact version reviewed. It is not a deployment approval.
The reviewer found a blocking issue in that reviewed version. Later cards explain the fixes and re-checks.
A request entering an ICP canister from a client. Size and caller filters reduce unnecessary work and cost.
A check comparing all tokens ever created by the Base contract with the bridge’s recorded mint activity before paying a return.
A proposed code change on GitHub, available for review but not yet merged into the main product.
An exact code version held unchanged while tests and reviewers assess it.
The opening characters of a file fingerprint. Here it identifies a compiled Wasm file, not a review round.
Two compiled files contain exactly the same bytes.
The canister library’s Rust unit-test suite, not the local end-to-end tests.
Rust’s automated checker for common code mistakes and quality issues.
Retrying test suites one at a time after simultaneous runs hit local test-infrastructure failures.
Short Git version identifier for the committed bridge design, plan and coordination documents.
Short Git version identifier for the new Base bridge token contract and its tests.
Short Git version identifier for the initial ICP bridge canister and local test harness.
Short Git version identifier for the Rumi Bridge web page.
Short Git version identifier for an early milestone that the first review examined.
Short Git version identifier for the first review round’s fixes.
Short Git version identifier for the cumulative-mint guard and the candidate used by the second review round.
Short Git version identifier for fixes to overlapping-tick double payments and lost-timer recovery.
Short Git version identifier for the second-round follow-up fixes assessed in the third review round.
Short Git version identifier for the final reviewed executable changes, including ingress bounds and timer fixes.
Short Git version identifier for later test and documentation improvements; the release executable stayed unchanged.
Short Git version identifier for the final local-delivery handoff accepted by Miles. It does not identify a live deployment.
Prefix of the compiled executable’s SHA-256 fingerprint for the earlier third-round review candidate.
Prefix of the final reviewed compiled executable’s SHA-256 fingerprint; tests were tied to that exact file.
Deliberately breaking small parts of code or evidence to verify that the tests detect the change.
Connect the bridge configuration to the exact expected Base token contract after validating its identity.
A configured upper limit, such as the amount of tokens that may exist or be issued.
Temporarily stop a supported operation without deleting existing claims.
A small, already-identified improvement left open after review. The three follow-ups here are being fixed before testnet testing.
Schedule the bridge's background check to run again soon, instead of waiting for its slower idle interval.
Read-only checks before a deployment: tools, identities, available cycles and test funds, signing keys and blockchain data services. Nothing is changed.
A written plan for one test deployment: exact targets, test assets, budget, commands, expected results and stop conditions, checked before anything public is changed.
The chain ID of Base Sepolia, Base's public test network. The bridge is limited to it for this test.
A separate ICP ledger issuing test icUSD with no value, used instead of the real icUSD ledger.
The one person or agent allowed to perform the public deployment steps, so no two attempts race.
The test-only Base Sepolia account key that would deploy the token contract. Creating it is on hold until it is explicitly authorized.
The exact compiled file that will be installed on ICP, after adding interface metadata and shrinking. Its fingerprint must match after install.
Proof level for the approved test run: new test canisters exist and are funded with the right controller, but no code is installed in them yet.
The point where the one person or agent running public steps waits for a tool or approval to respond. A pending request there is not retried another way.
After a request whose outcome is unknown, first read the authoritative state to learn what actually happened, and only then decide whether a new request is safe.
An answer that proves a request did nothing, so it is safe to fix the cause and try again. Unlike a stalled request, it leaves no unknown outcome.
Proof level for the approved test run: code is installed and its fingerprint read back matches the planned file.
Proof level for the approved test run: a Base transaction has a successful receipt, but it is not yet final and the operation is not yet settled.
Proof level for the approved test run: the bridge recorded the operation complete and independent ledger, Base and audit readbacks agree. It is not production proof.
Moving test icUSD from ICP to Base and then back from Base to ICP, checking balances and the audit at each end.
A throwaway local copy of the app that shows only the Bridge page and can only reach the test canisters. It is never committed or deployed.
A small script in the staging copy that blocks any network request to an ICP canister other than the two test canisters, and records what it saw.
Proof level for the staging copy: the page rendered against the test canisters and wallet screens were checked with a simulated, read-only wallet. It proves no real approval or transfer.
A simulated stand-in used in a test, here a read-only fake wallet that lets the page's wallet screens be checked without a real wallet.
Proof level for the staging copy: a real wallet sign-in worked and the page shows the signed-in account. It proves no transaction approval or transfer.
The ranked list of this board's sub-projects, with each one's status, what is blocking it and the next step. The order is the rank.
The Base wallet browser extension used for the browser test. It must be unlocked by its owner before the page can connect to it.
Board column for planned, scoped work that has not started. A queued card waits for the cards it depends on; it is not running and not finished.
The main Ethereum network. One of the nine planned destinations; nothing is deployed there.
A network that runs on top of Ethereum and settles back to it. A planned destination; nothing is deployed there.
Robinhood's own blockchain network, not the crypto trading in its brokerage app. A planned destination; its network details are being checked against official sources.
The Ethereum-compatible smart-contract layer of the Hyperliquid network, separate from HyperCore, Hyperliquid's own trading layer. A planned destination.
An Ethereum-compatible network. Rumi has separate lending code for it; a bridged token there would be new and kept apart from that code.
A fast network that is not Ethereum-compatible, with its own token standard and signing scheme. A planned destination.
A network built on the Move language that is not Ethereum-compatible. A planned destination; Rumi has no code for it yet.
The XRP Ledger. Rumi already accepts native XRP as collateral; a bridged dollar token there would be new and separate.
A checked-in description of one destination chain (network, token, decimals, signing, finality and wallets) with a source for each fact. Profiles start disabled and cannot turn anything on.
A priority status for queued future work that has not started and begins only when Rob or Miles opens that phase.

plainSummary: Moving test tokens to Base and back works outside the app; the browser test waits for Rob to sign in and unlock his wallet. Three more networks are ready in testing, the XRP Ledger version passes its local tests, and Solana and Sui are being built. Nothing new is switched on.
